strengths: Addresses a timely and important question in RL-based LLM reasoning: whether RL can genuinely expand reasoning capacity or merely sharpens existing base-model distributions, with direct engagement with recent skeptical findings (Yue et al., ProRL).
The proposed method (QuestA) is simple, easy to implement, and orthogonal to the underlying RL algorithm (only modifies input prompts), making it broadly applicable and low-overhead to adopt.

Strong and fairly comprehensive empirical results: consistent gains in both pass@1 and pass@k across multiple hard math benchmarks (AIME24/25, HMMT25, OlympiadBench, BRUMO25), applied to two different base models (DeepScaleR-1.5B and Nemotron-1.5B), achieving new SOTA among 1.5B models and even rivaling much larger 32B models on some benchmarks.

Pass@k curves (Figure 2) and unsolved-problem index tracking (Table 1) provide convincing qualitative evidence that the method expands genuine model capacity rather than just avoiding entropy collapse or reward hacking.
Training dynamics analysis (entropy, reward, length) shows the method does not suffer from entropy collapse, addressing a concern raised in prior work.
Includes an ablation on a different training dataset (OpenMathReasoning) showing the method generalizes across data sources, and limited OOD tests on non-math domains (coding, logic, QA).

Provides a theoretical framework (solution sets, model capacity sets) with formal propositions/theorems and proofs to motivate why partial-solution hints improve sample efficiency, going beyond purely empirical claims.
weaknesses: Core method novelty is limited: prepending partial ground-truth solutions as hints is conceptually close to existing curriculum/hint-based RL approaches (e.g., StepHint, cited but not empirically compared against), and the paper does not provide a direct empirical comparison to these closest baselines.

Only a single fixed hint ratio (p=50%) is used in the main experiments; the promised 'curriculum' aspect (varying p to adaptively reduce scaffolding) is explicitly left as future work, so a central part of the method's motivating narrative is untested.

The theoretical analysis, while formally stated, relies on a simplified tabular RL setting and an assumption (Definition 3.6/B.4) that a suitable hint exists with specific probability properties — this assumption is essentially posited rather than empirically verified for real math problems, limiting the practical rigor of the theory-to-practice connection.

Limited ablation depth: no analysis of sensitivity to hint ratio p, no isolation of QuestA's contribution versus the DAPO dynamic-sampling enhancements also used in training, and no exploration of alternative hint construction strategies.

Results appear to come from single training runs without reported variance/seeds, making it hard to assess statistical significance of the reported gains, especially in comparisons with baselines evaluated under potentially different setups.

OOD/generalization results (Table 3) are only reported for one of the two base models (DeepScaleR-1.5B), and the observed gains there are small (~0.8% average), somewhat undermining the generalization claims made in the text.

Several aspects of the paper have an unfinished, work-in-progress feel (e.g., explicit statements like 'prototype experiments,' 'currently working on extending this setup,' and an admission in the appendix that prior data curation was inaccurate), which raises concerns about the stability/reproducibility of the reported numbers.

Comparisons to much larger models (e.g., DeepSeek-R1-Distill-32B) are used to highlight impressiveness but involve different training data/pipelines, making such cross-model-family comparisons somewhat apples-to-oranges as evidence of the method's specific contribution.
Minor clarity/proofreading issues (typos such as 'transfors', 'Inifinite', stray text) suggest the manuscript could benefit from more careful revision.

strengths: Addresses a timely and well-motivated problem: whether RL can expand reasoning capacity on hard problems where base models fail, and whether pass@k/entropy collapse can be mitigated.

The proposed QuestA method (prepending partial solutions as hints during RL rollouts) is simple, modular, and easy to integrate into existing RL pipelines without changing reward or optimization machinery.
Strong reported numerical gains on 1.5B models across several competition math benchmarks (AIME24/25, HMMT25, Olympiad Bench, BRUMO25), with claimed new SOTA among 1.5B-scale models.
Includes pass@k curves and per-problem 'unsolved index' analysis that directly engages with the entropy-collapse/pass@k-degradation literature the paper is responding to.

Provides an ablation across two different source datasets (OpenR1 vs OpenMathReasoning) showing qualitatively similar training dynamics and final performance, suggesting some robustness to data source.
Reports training dynamics (reward, entropy, length) that are at least consistent with the paper's narrative of avoiding entropy collapse.
weaknesses: Critical missing baseline/ablation: the paper compares QuestA-trained models only against the original pretrained checkpoints (DeepScaleR-1.5B, Nemotron-1.5B), not against a 'continued RL training without hint augmentation for the same number of steps/compute' baseline. Since QuestA models undergo substantial additional RL training (750/500 steps) beyond the baseline checkpoints, it is impossible to attribute the reported gains specifically to the hint-augmentation idea rather than simply more RL training/compute. This confound undermines the central empirical claim of the paper.

The method is also confounded with DAPO-style enhancements (dynamic sampling, removed KL term) that are applied alongside QuestA; there is no ablation isolating the contribution of the hint augmentation itself from these other RL training tricks.

The theoretical contribution is informal and somewhat trivial: Proposition 3.1 (infinite monkey theorem applied to LLMs) and the bandit-style Theorem 3.8 operate in a toy tabular setting disconnected from the actual autoregressive, high-dimensional RL training setup used in experiments; the paper itself labels the main result 'informal,' and the gap between training-with-hint and inference-without-hint generalization (the actual empirical phenomenon) is not theoretically justified, only asserted.

Only a single model scale (1.5B) is evaluated; no experiments at larger scale (7B+) are provided to assess whether the method's benefits persist or diminish with scale, limiting claims of general applicability.

The hint ratio p=50% is fixed without any ablation sweeping this hyperparameter, despite the paper framing it as defining a 'curriculum'; the stated intention to explore curriculum scheduling is left as future work, suggesting incomplete investigation of the method's own design space.
Cross-domain (OOD) generalization results (Table 3) are weak (~0.8% average gain) and tested on only one of the two base models (DeepScaleR), undermining claims of broad applicability beyond math.

Comparisons against the DeepScaleR baseline appear potentially inconsistent/unclear regarding which checkpoint (Stage 2 vs Stage 3) and context length settings are used, raising concerns about fairness of the reported improvement.
No variance/seed analysis or confidence intervals are reported for the headline benchmark numbers, despite AIME-style benchmarks having very few problems (30) and high evaluation variance.

The paper has numerous typos and unpolished writing (e.g., 'transfors', 'Inifinite', 'Nematron', 'Desigining'), suggesting the submission was not carefully proofread, which raises concerns about overall rigor.
Table 1's 'unsolved problem index' analysis is based on only 23-30 problems per benchmark, offering limited statistical power to support claims of expanded reasoning capacity.
No comparison to other directly related hint/curriculum-based methods mentioned in related work (e.g., StepHint), despite these being close prior art addressing the same entropy/pass@k issues.

strengths: The core idea—injecting partial solutions into hard-example prompts during RL—is simple, intuitive, and easy to integrate into existing RLVR pipelines (GRPO/DAPO) without modifying the reward function or optimizer.

Strong empirical gains are shown on two different base models (DeepScaleR-1.5B and Nemotron-1.5B) across five competition math benchmarks, with consistent improvements in both pass@1 and pass@k, including new SOTA numbers among 1.5B models.

The paper directly engages with an important and timely debate (does RL expand reasoning capacity or just sharpen existing behavior / entropy collapse and pass@k degradation), and provides evidence (Fig. 2, Fig. 5, unsolved-problem indices in Table 1) that QuestA actually increases the solvable set rather than just reweighting existing capability.

A theoretical framework (solution set / model capacity set / hint-based sampling budget reduction) is provided to motivate why partial-solution hints should improve sample efficiency, giving the empirical method some principled grounding rather than being purely ad hoc.

Reasonable ablation on a second training dataset (OpenMathReasoning) shows the method is not overly sensitive to the specific data source, and training dynamics (entropy, reward, length) are reported to support the entropy-collapse-avoidance claim.
Implementation details (prompts, RL hyperparameters, low-variance pass@k estimator) are documented in the appendix, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to 1.5B-parameter models; no experiments at larger scales (7B+) are shown, so it's unclear whether gains persist or diminish as base model capability grows, limiting the generality/significance of the claims.

The theoretical analysis relies on strong, somewhat informal assumptions (e.g., Definition 3.6's existence of a hint with specific probability properties, the toy two-step decomposition argument for the sqrt speedup) and a tabular RL setting distinct from the actual autoregressive experiments; the connection between the formal results and the empirical method is more illustrative than rigorous.

No direct empirical comparison to closely related hint/curriculum-based methods discussed in related work (e.g., StepHint, curriculum RL from easy-to-hard), making it hard to assess QuestA's relative advantage over existing scaffolding approaches.
The hint ratio p is fixed at 50% without an ablation over different values, despite the paper itself noting this as an important design choice/curriculum dimension; no sensitivity analysis is given.

Cross-domain (OOD) generalization gains are marginal (~0.8% average on GPQA/Zebralogic/coding), and only tested for one model (DeepScaleR), raising questions about how specialized the benefit is to in-domain math reasoning.

AIME-style benchmarks have very small test sets (30 problems), and no variance/multiple-seed reporting is provided, so some of the reported improvements (e.g., a few percentage points) could be within noise; the pass@32 estimator mitigates but does not eliminate this concern.

Minor clarity/writing issues (e.g., typos such as 'transfors', 'Inifinite', inconsistent notation in Theorem 3.8 statement, confusing references to 'DeepScaleR-1.5B Stage 2' vs 'Stage 3') slightly undermine polish and could confuse readers trying to reproduce exact baselines.

Potential data leakage/contamination is not discussed: the training corpus (OpenR1-Math-220K) and evaluation sets (AIME24/25, HMMT, BRUMO) are both recent competition math sources, and no decontamination procedure is described.

strengths: Simple, practical, and easy-to-implement method (prepending partial ground-truth solutions as hints during RL rollouts) that requires no changes to the underlying RL algorithm or reward function, making it broadly applicable.
Strong empirical improvements on 1.5B-scale models, achieving new SOTA on AIME24/25, HMMT25, Olympiad Bench, and BRUMO25, with gains that persist even though hints are removed at evaluation time.

Thorough set of ablations: curriculum design (Partial-50 → Partial-25), hint vs. no-hint, different base models (Nemotron-1.5B, DeepScaleR-1.5B), and different training datasets (OpenR1 vs OpenMathReasoning), which help isolate the source of gains.

Pass@k analysis is a nice touch, directly engaging with the recent debate (Yue et al. 2025; Liu et al. 2025) about whether RL expands reasoning capacity, and shows QuestA avoids the pass@k degradation seen with standard RL on easy or all-hard data.
Entropy/training dynamics plots (Fig. 5, 10-16) provide some transparency into why the method works (no entropy collapse).

Attempt at theoretical grounding (capacity set / solution set formalism, sampling-budget theorems) gives an intuitive story for why hints reduce the effective sampling budget needed to discover correct trajectories.
weaknesses: The theoretical results (Def. 4.5, Thm 4.6) essentially assume the desired outcome (existence of a hint that boosts per-step solution probability to a specific threshold δp'), so the theory mostly restates the empirical motivation in symbolic form rather than deriving genuinely new predictive insight; the tabular/bandit reduction in Appendix B is far from the autoregressive LLM setting used in experiments.

A central conceptual concern is under-addressed: the hints are literal excerpts from DeepSeek-R1-generated solutions in OpenR1-Math-220K. Training on these hints could partly be a form of continued distillation from a strong teacher's solution text rather than genuine RL-driven capability expansion, which is in tension with the paper's framing around whether "RL expands reasoning capacity." No SFT-only baseline (training directly on the hint+solution pairs without RL) is provided to disentangle these effects.

All main experiments are on 1.5B-parameter models; no evidence is given that QuestA scales to larger models (7B/8B/32B) or that the gains hold as base model capability increases, limiting claims of general significance.

Missing comparisons against other recent hard-problem/curriculum RL methods explicitly cited in related work (e.g., ProRL/An et al. 2025, Parashar et al. 2025 curriculum RL, StepHint), making it hard to judge whether QuestA is meaningfully better than existing curriculum or entropy-preservation techniques rather than just an alternative not empirically pitted against them.

Benchmarks (AIME24/25, HMMT, BRUMO25, each ~30 problems) are small and potentially subject to contamination/memorization concerns for widely circulated competition problems; despite averaging over 32 samples this raises some concern about the robustness/significance of reported gains (e.g., +10-13 points).

Cross-domain OOD generalization results (Table 7) show only marginal gains (~0.8 avg), undermining the claim in the conclusion that QuestA could generalize to "competitive coding, software engineering, or other agentic tasks."

The two-stage curriculum schedule (100 steps at Partial-50, then switch to Partial-25) appears to be chosen somewhat ad hoc based on a single entropy-decline observation rather than a principled/adaptive scheduling rule, and the paper acknowledges the Partial-0 extension yielded no gains without much analysis of why.

Minor writing/technical issues: several typos ("adresses", "shwon", "vocaboluary", "we easily the following lower bound"), and some numeric inconsistencies could benefit from more careful proofreading.

strengths: The empirical results are strong and consistent: applying QuestA to Nemotron-1.5B and DeepScaleR-1.5B yields sizable gains on AIME24/25, HMMT, Olympiad Bench, and BRUMO25, with new SOTA numbers among 1.5B models.

The pass@k analysis (Fig. 2, 7, 8, 17) is a nice diagnostic that directly engages with the recent 'does RL expand reasoning capacity' debate, showing QuestA avoids the pass@k degradation reported by Yue et al. and Liu et al.

Extensive ablations are provided: curriculum vs. single-stage augmentation, with/without hints, different base models (Nemotron vs DeepScaleR), and different source datasets (OpenR1 vs OpenMathReasoning), which strengthens confidence that the effect is not a one-off artifact.
The method is simple and orthogonal to the underlying RL algorithm (plug-and-play on top of GRPO/DAPO pipelines), making it easy to adopt in practice.

The paper is transparent about training dynamics (reward, length, entropy curves) across many configurations in the appendix, aiding interpretability of why the method works (denser reward signal, preserved entropy).
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core idea of injecting partial/ground-truth solution hints to scaffold RL on hard problems is closely related to existing curriculum/hint-based RL work the paper itself cites (e.g., StepHint, 'Curriculum RL from easy to hard'), but no direct empirical comparison to these baselines is provided, making it hard to assess the marginal contribution.

The theoretical analysis (Section 4, Theorems 4.4/4.6) relies on a simplified tabular bandit-style setup with strong, unverified assumptions (e.g., Definition 4.5's existence of hints with specific probability bounds, Assumption 4.3) that do not clearly map onto the actual autoregressive LLM RL setting used in experiments; the theory mostly formalizes an intuitive point (hints reduce the effective search space) rather than offering non-trivial predictive insight, and is not empirically validated (e.g., the claimed sqrt(1/δp) speedup is never measured).

Evaluation is restricted to a small set of competition math benchmarks (AIME, HMMT, BRUMO, Olympiad Bench) with modest problem counts, which can produce high-variance results; no contamination analysis is given despite using benchmarks that are easy to leak into large pretraining/SFT corpora.

Cross-domain generalization (Table 7) is weak/marginal (GPQA, Zebralogic, coding), undercutting the conclusion's claim that the approach 'can potentially be generalized to other domains such as competitive coding, software engineering.'

Key design choices (50%→25% hint curriculum, 100-step cutoff for switching, 0-4 correct out of 8 resampling threshold) appear heuristically tuned without principled justification or sensitivity analysis beyond a single ablation.

Scale is limited to 1.5B parameter models only; it is unclear whether the benefits persist or diminish at larger scales where base-model capability is already higher, limiting the generality of the state-of-the-art claims.

The data curation/augmentation pipeline (two-stage difficulty filtering, iterative re-sampling with the in-training model) adds substantial complexity and compute overhead that is not clearly quantified or compared against simpler baselines (e.g., plain hard-example RL with longer training, or easier curriculum schedules) on an equal compute budget.

Minor writing issues (typos such as 'adresses', 'shwon', 'formallize') and some overstated claims (e.g., 'our theoretical analysis explains why...' when the theory's assumptions are not shown to hold) reduce overall polish and rigor.

strengths: Simple, practical, and easily integrable method (prepending partial ground-truth solutions as hints) that requires no change to RL algorithm, reward function, or architecture.
Strong empirical results: new SOTA among 1.5B models on AIME24/25, HMMT25, Olympiad Bench, and BRUMO25, with substantial absolute gains over the Nemotron-1.5B baseline.

Extensive ablations: curriculum (50%->25%) vs. single-stage hinting, with/without hints at training time, transfer across datasets (OpenR1 vs OpenMathReasoning) and across base models (Nemotron vs DeepScaleR), providing good robustness evidence for the core claim.

Directly engages with and provides counter-evidence to the recent narrative that RLVR cannot expand reasoning capacity beyond the base model, showing pass@k preservation/improvement rather than degradation.

Reasonably clear identification of the easy-vs-hard prompt tradeoff (fast but shallow learning vs. slow but capacity-expanding learning), which motivates the method well and is backed by a controlled experiment (Figure 2/3).
Good transparency: detailed appendix with training dynamics (reward, length, entropy curves), evaluation protocol (unbiased pass@k estimator), and prompt templates, aiding reproducibility.
Some investigation of generalization: hints removed at test time still yield gains, and mild OOD transfer to coding/logic/knowledge benchmarks is reported.
weaknesses: Theoretical analysis (Section 4) relies on a highly simplified tabular/bandit-like setup with strong idealized assumptions (Definition 4.5's existence of hints with specific probability properties) that do not clearly map onto the actual autoregressive LLM setting; it reads more as a stylized intuition-building exercise than a rigorous explanation of why QuestA specifically (vs. any curriculum method) works.

Missing direct empirical comparison with closely related hint/curriculum-based RL baselines explicitly discussed in related work (e.g., StepHint, easy-to-hard curriculum RL by Parashar et al.), which would better establish the specific contribution of using ground-truth partial solutions over other hinting/curriculum strategies.

The reported OOD generalization (Table 7) shows very small gains (+0.78 avg) on GPQA/Zebralogic/coding benchmarks that could plausibly be within noise, yet the text frames this as meaningful cross-domain generalization.

All main experiments are restricted to 1.5B-scale models; no evidence is provided on whether the benefits of QuestA persist, diminish, or grow at larger model scales, limiting claims about general applicability.

The choice of specific hint percentages (50% then 25%, stopping before 0%) appears to be based on limited exploratory tuning rather than systematic justification; the negative result for extending to Partial-0 is reported but not well explained mechanistically.

Reliance on mixing self-evaluated numbers for the proposed method with officially reported numbers for some baselines (DeepSeek-R1-Distill, Qwen3) introduces potential inconsistency in evaluation protocol/benchmark versions.
Minor writing/typo issues (e.g., 'shwon', 'adresses', 'vocaboluary', 'sodlved', 'we easily the following') suggest the manuscript could benefit from a more careful proofreading pass.

The method depends on access to high-quality step-by-step reference solutions for hint construction, which may limit applicability to domains lacking such annotated solution trajectories (acknowledged only briefly as future work).
